The Harbor Survey
The harbor survey began in the spring, when the ice had cleared from the inner channel and
the pilots could take the launch out at first light. Each morning the crew measured the depth at
forty marked stations, wrote the readings in a bound log, and compared them with the charts
drawn twenty years before.
By the middle of summer the pattern was plain. The channel had shifted toward the eastern
breakwater, and the shoal off the ferry landing had grown by almost a meter. The pilots had
known this for years from the feel of the boats, but the survey gave them numbers they could
show the port council.
The council voted in the autumn to dredge the eastern approach and to move two of the
channel buoys. The survey crew stayed on through the winter to check the work, and their
final log, bound in green cloth, is kept in the harbor office today.

Readings are totals for each quarter, rounded to the nearest millimeter.

Seasonal Water Levels
The reservoir rises through the wet months and falls through the dry ones. The chart below
shows the average level at the end of each season over the last ten years.

Figure 1: average reservoir level at the end of winter, spring, summer, and autumn.
The lowest level comes at the end of summer, when demand is highest and the inflow is
smallest.

Notes on Garden Soil

Good garden soil holds water without staying wet. A handful squeezed in the palm should keep its shape for a moment and then crumble when pressed with a thumb.

Clay soil drains slowly and warms late in the spring. Working in leaf mold and coarse sand over several seasons opens it up and lets roots reach deeper.

Sandy soil drains quickly and loses its nutrients in heavy rain. Compost added each autumn gives it body and feeds the worms that keep it loose.

Most vegetables grow best in soil that is slightly acid. A simple test kit from the hardware store shows the level in a few minutes.

Lime raises the level slowly and should go on in the autumn, so the winter rain can carry it down. Sulfur lowers it, but more slowly still.

Whatever the soil, a layer of mulch keeps it cool in summer, holds moisture through dry weeks, and smothers most of the weeds before they start.

The Harbor Survey

The harbor survey began in the spring, when the ice had cleared from the inner channel and the pilots could take the launch out at first light. Each morning the crew measured the depth at forty marked stations, wrote the readings in a bound log, and compared them with the charts drawn twenty years before.

By the middle of summer the pattern was plain. The channel had shifted toward the eastern breakwater, and the shoal off the old ferry landing had grown by almost a meter. The pilots had known this for years from the feel of the boats, but the survey gave them numbers they could show the port council.

The council voted in the autumn to dredge the eastern approach and to move two of the channel buoys. The survey crew stayed on through the winter to check the work, and their final log, bound in green cloth, is kept in the harbor office today.

Notes on Garden Soil

Good garden soil should be rich in organic matter and well-drained. A well-structured soil is essential for healthy plant growth. The soil should be loose and friable, allowing roots to penetrate easily and air to reach them.

The soil should also have a good balance of sand, silt, and clay. Too much sand can lead to rapid drainage and nutrient leaching, while too much clay can cause poor drainage and compaction.

Adding organic matter, such as compost or well-rotted manure, can improve soil structure and fertility. This helps to increase water retention and provide essential nutrients for plants.

The pH of the soil is also important. Most plants prefer a slightly acidic to neutral pH. If your soil is too acidic or too alkaline, you can adjust it by adding lime or sulfur.

Regularly testing your soil can help you understand its nutrient levels and pH, allowing you to make informed decisions about soil amendments.

Vegetables grow best in well-drained, fertile soil. A single layer of mulch can help to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and improve soil structure over time.

Mulch can be made from various materials, such as straw, wood chips, or leaves. Choose a mulch that is appropriate for your garden and the types of plants you are growing.

Applying mulch can also help to regulate soil temperature, protecting roots from extreme heat or cold.

In summary, healthy garden soil is the foundation of a successful garden. By understanding your soil's needs and taking steps to improve it, you can create a thriving environment for your plants.
